programs.name: Maryland Department of Aging (State Unit on Aging)
programs.federal_name: Older Americans Act Title III-B and Title III-E (Area Agencies on Aging)
programs.about: Your local Area Agency on Aging may pay for a home safety check or small fixes like grab bars. Find yours through the Eldercare Locator at www.eldercare.gov or (800) 677-1116.

programs.name: Maryland Technology Assistance Program
Maryland Centers for Independent Living
VA Specially Adapted Housing (SAH), Special Housing Adaptation (SHA), Temporary Residence Adaptation (TRA) and HISA grants
programs.federal_name: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs housing grants
programs.about: HISA details are at http://www.prosthetics.va.gov/psas/HISA2.asp; SAH staff can be reached at (877) 827-3702.

programs.name: Maryland State Department of Education, Division of Rehabilitation Services
Health insurance (incl. Medicare Advantage), long-term care insurance and life insurance
Maryland Medicaid
programs.federal_name: Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) Waivers
programs.about: Maryland Medicaid runs waiver programs that can pay for home changes like ramps or bathroom updates so a person can stay out of a nursing home. They are for people with low income who are older or who have long-term health conditions. Ask the state Medicaid office which waiver fits.

programs.name: Maryland Money Follows the Person Program
programs.about: This Medicaid program helps people move from a nursing home back to a home in the community. Help can include getting the new home ready, and services differ by state.

programs.name: Social Security Plan for Achieving Self-Support (PASS) and Impairment-Related Work Expenses (IRWE)
programs.about: People on SSI or SSDI who work may be able to set aside money or count work-related costs, including some home changes, without losing as much of their benefit. TTY 1-800-325-0778.

programs.name: Community Development Block Grants (CDBG) - Maryland grantees
programs.about: Many cities and counties use CDBG money for home repair programs; ask your local housing or community development office.

programs.name: HOME Program - Maryland grantees
programs.about: Search the HUD Exchange grantee list by state to see which local governments offer HOME-funded repair help.

programs.name: Local Housing/Neighborhood Agencies (Neighborhood Housing Services)
programs.about: Local nonprofit housing groups, such as NeighborWorks members, may give repair advice, low-cost loans or small grants. Search your city name plus "Neighborhood Housing Services" or use the NeighborWorks directory.

programs.name: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
programs.about: The state housing finance agency may offer low-interest or deferred loans for home repairs, and it funds housing for older adults and people with disabilities. Check its site for current repair or accessibility programs.

programs.name: USDA Rural Development - Maryland offices
programs.federal_name: USDA Section 504 Home Repair loans and grants (and Section 533 Housing Preservation Grants)
programs.about: Maryland has a USDA Rural Development area office in Hagerstown and satellite offices in La Plata and Upper Marlboro.

programs.name: Maryland Weatherization Assistance Program
programs.about: In Maryland this program is run by the Department of Housing and Community Development.

programs.name: FHA Title I Home Improvement and 203(k) Rehabilitation loans
programs.about: Find a lender that offers Title I or 203(k) loans at https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/housing/sfh/lender/lenderlist.

programs.name: Home Equity Line of Credit
programs.about: A homeowner can borrow against the home's value as needed to pay for changes. The loan must be paid back with interest, and the home is the collateral. Ask a local bank or credit union.

programs.name: Home Equity Loan
programs.about: This is a second loan on the home, paid back on top of the first mortgage. It can cover a larger project in one lump sum. Ask a local bank.

programs.name: Lender Unsecured/Personal Loans
programs.about: A personal loan can pay for smaller jobs and does not put a lien on the home, so renters can use it too. Approval depends on income, debt and credit.

programs.name: Mortgage Refinancing
programs.about: Replacing the current mortgage with a new, larger one can free up cash for home changes if the home has enough equity. Ask a local lender.

programs.name: Remodeler Donated Financing
programs.about: Some contractors donate part of a job, their labor or materials, often as community giving. Ask your remodeler if they do this.

programs.name: Remodeler Referred Financing
programs.about: Many contractors work with finance companies and can set up a loan for the project. It can be quick, but compare the rate with a bank.

programs.name: Reverse Equity Mortgage (HECM)
programs.about: Talk with a HUD-approved counselor first; see also http://www.reversemortgage.org and https://www.ncoa.org/economic-security/home-equity/reverse-mortgages/reverse-mortgage-counseling/.

programs.name: Secured Loans Against Homeowner's Bank Accounts
programs.about: A bank may lend against a certificate of deposit (CD) you hold there, usually up to part of its value. This can work for smaller projects. Ask your bank.

programs.name: Secured Loans Against Homeowner's Financial Investment Accounts (Margin Loan)
programs.about: Some investment firms let you borrow against the stocks or funds in your account. The money can sometimes go to home projects, but the loan carries market risk. Ask your bank or broker.

programs.name: Civic, Advocacy, Religious, and Trade Groups
programs.about: Churches, service clubs, scout troops and builder groups sometimes build ramps or raise money for home changes. Call 211 to find groups near you.

programs.name: Maryland Victims of Crime Fund
programs.federal_name: Crime Victims' Benefits (U.S. Department of Justice)
programs.about: If a crime left someone hurt or disabled, the state victim compensation program may help pay for home access changes. It pays only what insurance or the offender does not.

programs.name: Social Security Title XX Social Services Block Grant (SSBG)
programs.about: States use this block grant for local social services, which can include basic changes like a ramp or grab bars. It mostly helps households already on public assistance; ask your local social services office.

programs.name: Maryland Workers' Compensation Commission
programs.about: If a job injury makes daily life at home hard, workers' comp may pay for home changes or help with a more suitable home. File through the employer's insurance claim.

programs.name: Internal Revenue Service - medical expense deduction, capital gains basis and business deduction
State/Local Taxes - sales tax and property tax exemptions
programs.about: Some states or counties waive sales tax on ramp materials or lift equipment, or keep accessibility work from raising property taxes. Check with the Maryland revenue department and your county tax office.

programs.name: Independent Living Tax Credit
programs.about: Maryland taxpayers who make a home more accessible can get a state tax credit of up to half the cost, capped at $5,000. The home can be your own, a relative's, or a rental. The state housing department runs it.

programs.name: Howard County Senior Tax Credit and Aging in Place Tax Credit
programs.about: Howard County offers property tax credits for older homeowners, including one tied to aging in place. Check the county tax credit page for current rules.

programs.name: Montgomery County Design for Life Tax Incentive
programs.about: Montgomery County offers a property tax incentive for homes with accessible design features. See the county page for current rules.

notes: Maryland has a state Independent Living Tax Credit (up to 50% of cost, max $5,000) plus county property tax incentives in Howard and Montgomery counties.
